title: Functions, graphs and composition

chapters.label: Start with the idea
chapters.name: StartWithTheIdea
chapters.narration: Imagine following one pixel through preprocessing: first scale it, then shift it. Each operation consumes the previous output. Function composition gives a precise language for this sequence, including an order that you can trace with one concrete number.

chapters.label: Specify the two functions
chapters.name: SetUpTheCalculation
chapters.narration: A function has an input and an output. Here one scales its input and the other shifts it.

chapters.label: Read composition from the inside
chapters.name: FollowTheOperation
chapters.narration: The function nearest the input acts first. The composition symbol does not mean multiply the functions.

chapters.label: Pause and predict
chapters.name: PredictTheChange
chapters.narration: For which scale will the two orders agree? Pause here and make a prediction before continuing.

chapters.label: Finish both possible orders
chapters.name: CheckTheNumbers
chapters.narration: The first order adds three after scaling. The second scales the added three as well. For our starting inputs, Scale then shift: 11. Shift then scale: 14.

chapters.label: Explain the difference
chapters.name: ExplainTheResult
chapters.narration: The orders agree at scale one. A particular agreement does not mean all transformations commute.

chapters.label: Connect it to computer vision
chapters.name: ConnectTheLesson
chapters.narration: Preprocessing order is part of the model specification. Write intermediate values when a nested expression feels hard to follow.

title: Sums, averages and error

chapters.label: Start with the idea
chapters.name: StartWithTheIdea
chapters.narration: A prediction error first needs a reference: prediction minus observed target. That signed residual tells you whether a model is too high or too low. Averaging signed residuals can conceal mistakes because opposite signs cancel.

chapters.label: Define the residuals
chapters.name: SetUpTheCalculation
chapters.narration: A residual is prediction minus target. Its sign tells us the direction of the error.

chapters.label: Square before adding
chapters.name: FollowTheOperation
chapters.narration: The square treats equal positive and negative mistakes equally and prevents cancellation.

chapters.label: Pause and predict
chapters.name: PredictTheChange
chapters.narration: Will reversing the sign change the mean squared error? Pause here and make a prediction before continuing.

chapters.label: Average over observations
chapters.name: CheckTheNumbers
chapters.narration: The denominator is the number of residuals, including zero residuals. It is not the number of mistakes. For our starting inputs, Signed residual: -2. Squared-error sum: 4. MSE: 1.3333.

chapters.label: Check how scale changes loss
chapters.name: ExplainTheResult
chapters.narration: Doubling errors quadruples squared error. Loss units are the square of the target units.

chapters.label: Connect it to computer vision
chapters.name: ConnectTheLesson
chapters.narration: A loss can become smaller through better predictions or simply through rescaling the target. Compare models under the same objective and units.

title: Powers, logarithms and confidence

chapters.label: Start with the idea
chapters.name: StartWithTheIdea
chapters.narration: A binary classifier begins with a score: a real number expressing which side of its decision boundary an input lies on. Sigmoid converts that score into a class-1 probability. The score and probability are different quantities, so they have different allowed ranges and different meanings.

chapters.label: Start with an unrestricted score
chapters.name: SetUpTheCalculation
chapters.narration: A score can be negative or greater than one. It is not yet a probability, so taking the logarithm of the score would be the wrong operation.

chapters.label: Map score to class-1 probability
chapters.name: FollowTheOperation
chapters.narration: The exponential is positive, so the denominator exceeds one. This keeps the output strictly between zero and one for any finite score.

chapters.label: Pause and predict
chapters.name: PredictTheChange
chapters.narration: Keep the score fixed and change the observed class. Which quantities will change? Pause here and make a prediction before continuing.

chapters.label: Keep the observed class in view
chapters.name: CheckTheNumbers
chapters.narration: The model has two complementary probabilities. The loss uses the one assigned to the class that actually occurred. For our starting inputs, Class 1 probability: 0.75026. True-class probability: 0.75026. Negative log loss: 0.28734.

chapters.label: Measure how surprising that class is
chapters.name: ExplainTheResult
chapters.narration: Taking the negative logarithm produces a nonnegative penalty. A small true-class probability creates a large penalty; increasing it reduces the loss.

chapters.label: Connect it to computer vision
chapters.name: ConnectTheLesson
chapters.narration: Trace z → sigmoid(z) → probability of the observed class → negative logarithm. Do not take the logarithm of the score or forget the target.

title: Vectors as positions, displacements and features

chapters.label: Start with the idea
chapters.name: StartWithTheIdea
chapters.narration: Coordinates make geometric statements numerical. A position is meaningful relative to an origin and axes. A displacement compares two positions measured in the same convention and records the change coordinate by coordinate.

chapters.label: Choose a coordinate convention
chapters.name: SetUpTheCalculation
chapters.narration: Both positions use the same origin, axis directions and coordinate units. Otherwise subtraction would not describe the intended move.

chapters.label: Subtract coordinate by coordinate
chapters.name: FollowTheOperation
chapters.narration: The first coordinate is horizontal change; the second is vertical change. A negative change means movement opposite the positive axis.

chapters.label: Pause and predict
chapters.name: PredictTheChange
chapters.narration: Can the displacement change while its vertical component stays constant? Pause here and make a prediction before continuing.

chapters.label: Separate displacement from distance
chapters.name: CheckTheNumbers
chapters.narration: The displacement is a vector. Its Euclidean norm is a single nonnegative distance. For our starting inputs, Horizontal change: 3. Vertical change: -2. Distance: 3.6056.

chapters.label: Recover the endpoint
chapters.name: ExplainTheResult
chapters.narration: Adding a displacement to a position gives another position. Shifting the origin changes both positions but leaves their difference unchanged.

chapters.label: Connect it to computer vision
chapters.name: ConnectTheLesson
chapters.narration: Check what each coordinate represents before adding vectors. Feature vectors and spatial positions share notation but need not share a geometric meaning.

title: Matrices as maps and composition

chapters.label: Start with the idea
chapters.name: StartWithTheIdea
chapters.narration: Read a matrix row as a recipe for one output coordinate. Each row takes a weighted sum of all input components, and the collection of rows produces the output vector. Matrix multiplication is therefore a map, not multiplication of matching entries.

chapters.label: Check dimensions before multiplying
chapters.name: SetUpTheCalculation
chapters.narration: The inner dimensions match. The result has two rows and one column; it is an output vector.

chapters.label: Use a row as a weighted sum
chapters.name: FollowTheOperation
chapters.narration: A row describes one output coordinate. Every entry in that row weights a corresponding input coordinate.

chapters.label: Pause and predict
chapters.name: PredictTheChange
chapters.narration: What information disappears when the horizontal scale becomes zero? Pause here and make a prediction before continuing.

chapters.label: Compute the other coordinate
chapters.name: CheckTheNumbers
chapters.narration: The second row keeps the vertical coordinate. This example stretches horizontally and adds a shear. For our starting inputs, Output x: 7. Output y: 3. Area scale: 2.

chapters.label: Interpret the map geometrically
chapters.name: ExplainTheResult
chapters.narration: The determinant describes signed area scaling for this square map. At zero, one input direction collapses and the map is not invertible.

chapters.label: Connect it to computer vision
chapters.name: ConnectTheLesson
chapters.narration: A layer’s numerical entries, input convention and output dimensions together define its behaviour.

title: Independence, bases, rank and null spaces

chapters.label: Start with the idea
chapters.name: StartWithTheIdea
chapters.narration: A matrix may have many entries without preserving every input direction. Rank counts independent directions in its outputs. The null space contains input changes that the matrix sends to zero, so these changes cannot be recovered from the output.

chapters.label: Inspect the map
chapters.name: SetUpTheCalculation
chapters.narration: The second output coordinate is always zero. Although there are two input coordinates, only one independent output direction survives.

chapters.label: Find an input that disappears
chapters.name: FollowTheOperation
chapters.narration: Substitute this nonzero vector into the map: the first-row contributions cancel, and the second row is already zero.

chapters.label: Pause and predict
chapters.name: PredictTheChange
chapters.narration: Will changing the coefficient change the number of lost directions, or only their orientation? Pause here and make a prediction before continuing.

chapters.label: Count preserved and lost dimensions
chapters.name: CheckTheNumbers
chapters.narration: Rank counts independent output directions. Nullity counts independent input directions sent to zero. For our starting inputs, Rank: 1. Nullity: 1. Null x-coordinate: -1.

chapters.label: Check rank-nullity
chapters.name: ExplainTheResult
chapters.narration: Adding a null vector to any input leaves its output unchanged. This demonstrates the information loss directly.

chapters.label: Connect it to computer vision
chapters.name: ConnectTheLesson
chapters.narration: Information loss is a property of the map. A clever inverse algorithm cannot recover a direction that every output erased.

captionTiming: Proportional word timing within recorded chapters

title: Exact, inconsistent and underdetermined systems

chapters.label: Start with the idea
chapters.name: StartWithTheIdea
chapters.narration: An exact system asks for an input that satisfies every observation simultaneously. If two equations demand different values for the same expression, no input can satisfy both. This is inconsistency, even if the coefficient matrix has a familiar shape.

chapters.label: Write the observed constraints
chapters.name: SetUpTheCalculation
chapters.narration: Both equations ask about the same sum. They cannot determine x and y individually.

chapters.label: Check exact consistency
chapters.name: FollowTheOperation
chapters.narration: Consistency asks whether all equations can hold simultaneously. Counting equations alone does not answer that question.

chapters.label: Pause and predict
chapters.name: PredictTheChange
chapters.narration: When the observations agree, do they determine both unknowns uniquely? Pause here and make a prediction before continuing.

chapters.label: Fit the identifiable sum instead
chapters.name: CheckTheNumbers
chapters.narration: The least-squares compromise is the mean of the two requested sums. This changes the objective from exact matching to minimum squared error. For our starting inputs, First target: 1. Second target: 2. Fitted sum: 1.5.

chapters.label: Inspect the remaining error
chapters.name: ExplainTheResult
chapters.narration: The residual entries sum to zero. Even after fitting, x and y remain underdetermined: any pair with this fitted sum is a minimizer.

chapters.label: Connect it to computer vision
chapters.name: ConnectTheLesson
chapters.narration: Check consistency, identifiable quantities and uniqueness separately before choosing a solver.

captionTiming: Proportional word timing within recorded chapters

title: Least squares as projection

chapters.label: Start with the idea
chapters.name: StartWithTheIdea
chapters.narration: A model cannot produce every possible observation vector. A constant model, for example, can only produce outputs whose entries are all equal. Fitting chooses the point in this small output space closest to the observed targets.

chapters.label: Choose a deliberately small model
chapters.name: SetUpTheCalculation
chapters.narration: The model predicts the same value for every observation. Its representable outputs lie on the line spanned by the all-ones vector.

chapters.label: Minimize the squared distances
chapters.name: FollowTheOperation
chapters.narration: Differentiating the sum of squared residuals and setting the derivative to zero gives the sample mean.

chapters.label: Pause and predict
chapters.name: PredictTheChange
chapters.narration: If one target increases by three, how much will the fitted constant move? Pause here and make a prediction before continuing.

chapters.label: Compute the residual vector
chapters.name: CheckTheNumbers
chapters.narration: These are prediction-minus-observation residuals. Individual residuals can be nonzero at the best fit. For our starting inputs, Fitted constant: 2. Squared residual sum: 2.

chapters.label: Test the projection condition
chapters.name: ExplainTheResult
chapters.narration: The residual is orthogonal to the only model direction. It cannot be reduced further by shifting every prediction together.

chapters.label: Connect it to computer vision
chapters.name: ConnectTheLesson
chapters.narration: Inspect the residual pattern as well as the fitted parameters. A best fit can still be a poor model of the data.

title: QR, pseudoinverses and numerical conditioning

chapters.label: Start with the idea
chapters.name: StartWithTheIdea
chapters.narration: Some maps preserve one direction strongly and another only weakly. Recovering an input then requires undoing a very small scaling, which can amplify noise and rounding. The condition number measures this imbalance in a stated norm.

chapters.label: Identify the singular-value extremes
chapters.name: SetUpTheCalculation
chapters.narration: Both values are positive in this example, so the map has full rank. A small minimum value marks a weakly preserved direction.

chapters.label: Measure relative sensitivity
chapters.name: FollowTheOperation
chapters.narration: The condition number compares strongest to weakest scaling. A larger ratio means that relative perturbations can be strongly amplified.

chapters.label: Pause and predict
chapters.name: PredictTheChange
chapters.narration: What happens to sensitivity as the smallest singular value approaches zero? Pause here and make a prediction before continuing.

chapters.label: See what normal equations change
chapters.name: CheckTheNumbers
chapters.narration: For a full-column-rank matrix, singular values are squared in the Gram matrix. This can worsen numerical sensitivity. For our starting inputs, Condition number: 20. Gram condition number: 400.

chapters.label: Choose the computation accordingly
chapters.name: ExplainTheResult
chapters.narration: QR and SVD solve fitting problems without explicitly forming the Gram matrix. This improves the numerical route; it does not remove sensitivity inherent in the original data.

chapters.label: Connect it to computer vision
chapters.name: ConnectTheLesson
chapters.narration: A tiny residual does not guarantee accurate recovered parameters in a poorly conditioned problem.

captionTiming: Proportional word timing within recorded chapters

title: Regularization and the cost of overfitting

chapters.label: Start with the idea
chapters.name: StartWithTheIdea
chapters.narration: Fitting only the training observations can encourage complicated or unstable parameter choices. A regularizer adds a cost for a chosen property, such as large weight magnitude. It changes the optimization objective rather than merely changing the way a solver computes it.

chapters.label: Write a one-parameter objective
chapters.name: SetUpTheCalculation
chapters.narration: The first term rewards matching the observation. The second charges for weight magnitude; its coefficient states the tradeoff.

chapters.label: Differentiate both terms
chapters.name: FollowTheOperation
chapters.narration: The penalty contributes to the derivative too. Minimizing only the data term would give a different answer.

chapters.label: Pause and predict
chapters.name: PredictTheChange
chapters.narration: Will the training error necessarily decrease when the penalty gets stronger? Pause here and make a prediction before continuing.

chapters.label: Solve the stationary equation
chapters.name: CheckTheNumbers
chapters.narration: Collecting the terms in w gives this solution. The positive curvature makes it the unique global minimizer in this example. For our starting inputs, Unpenalized fit: 2. Regularized fit: 1. Data error: 1.

chapters.label: Measure the compromise
chapters.name: ExplainTheResult
chapters.narration: A larger penalty can increase training error while reducing weight size. Validation, rather than training fit alone, decides whether this preference is useful.

chapters.label: Connect it to computer vision
chapters.name: ConnectTheLesson
chapters.narration: Better training fit and better performance on unseen data are separate outcomes.

title: Eigenvectors and repeated transformations

chapters.label: Start with the idea
chapters.name: StartWithTheIdea
chapters.narration: An eigenvector is a nonzero direction that a square matrix maps to a scalar multiple of itself. The direction’s line survives the transformation even when its length changes or its orientation reverses.

chapters.label: Choose an eigenvector
chapters.name: SetUpTheCalculation
chapters.narration: This nonzero vector lies along the first coordinate axis. The diagonal map does not mix it with the second axis.

chapters.label: Apply the map once
chapters.name: FollowTheOperation
chapters.narration: The vector remains on the same line. The scalar multiplier is its eigenvalue.

chapters.label: Pause and predict
chapters.name: PredictTheChange
chapters.narration: How will a negative eigenvalue behave after one, two and three applications? Pause here and make a prediction before continuing.

chapters.label: Apply it three times
chapters.name: CheckTheNumbers
chapters.narration: Each application multiplies the previous coefficient by the same eigenvalue. Repeated action therefore produces a power. For our starting inputs, Eigenvalue: 2. After three maps: 8.

chapters.label: Interpret sign and magnitude
chapters.name: ExplainTheResult
chapters.narration: Magnitude below one contracts; magnitude above one grows. A negative eigenvalue alternates the orientation on successive applications. At zero the direction disappears.

chapters.label: Connect it to computer vision
chapters.name: ConnectTheLesson
chapters.narration: Eigenvalues describe signed action on special directions. Singular values instead describe nonnegative stretching and apply to rectangular maps too.

captionTiming: Proportional word timing within recorded chapters

title: SVD and low-rank structure

chapters.label: Start with the idea
chapters.name: StartWithTheIdea
chapters.narration: Singular-value decomposition describes a matrix as a rotation or change of orthonormal coordinates, followed by nonnegative stretching, followed by another coordinate change. It works for rectangular matrices as well as square ones.

chapters.label: Start with ordered singular values
chapters.name: SetUpTheCalculation
chapters.narration: The restriction keeps the first direction at least as strong as the second. Singular values describe stretching, not signed eigenvalue reversal.

chapters.label: Keep the strongest direction
chapters.name: FollowTheOperation
chapters.narration: A rank-one approximation preserves the first singular component and discards the other.

chapters.label: Pause and predict
chapters.name: PredictTheChange
chapters.narration: What fraction of squared matrix energy remains when both singular values are equal? Pause here and make a prediction before continuing.

chapters.label: Measure discarded structure
chapters.name: CheckTheNumbers
chapters.narration: The Frobenius norm is the square root of the sum of squared entries. Its squared error equals the sum of squared discarded singular values. For our starting inputs, Retained singular value: 4. Discarded singular value: 1. Retained energy: 0.94118.

chapters.label: Calculate retained energy
chapters.name: ExplainTheResult
chapters.narration: This is a squared-norm energy fraction. A large fraction does not guarantee that the discarded detail is irrelevant to a CV task.

chapters.label: Connect it to computer vision
chapters.name: ConnectTheLesson
chapters.narration: Choose approximation rank using the intended task and reconstruction behaviour, rather than a large energy percentage alone.

title: PCA, centering and covariance

chapters.label: Start with the idea
chapters.name: StartWithTheIdea
chapters.narration: A cloud of observations may vary strongly along one line and weakly across it. PCA centres each feature, then chooses orthogonal directions that capture the most sample variation. The mean must be kept if you later reconstruct the original observations.

chapters.label: Centre three observations
chapters.name: SetUpTheCalculation
chapters.narration: Rows are observations and columns are features. This symmetric example already has a zero feature mean.

chapters.label: Compute sample covariance
chapters.name: FollowTheOperation
chapters.narration: The denominator is n minus one for this sample-covariance convention. Off-diagonal entries measure joint variation.

chapters.label: Pause and predict
chapters.name: PredictTheChange
chapters.narration: Can the principal direction change while the data remains one-dimensional? Pause here and make a prediction before continuing.

chapters.label: Find the leading unit direction
chapters.name: CheckTheNumbers
chapters.narration: All three centred points lie on one line. Its normalized direction is the first principal axis; the perpendicular variance is zero. For our starting inputs, Leading variance: 5. Second variance: 0.

chapters.label: Project into one coordinate
chapters.name: ExplainTheResult
chapters.narration: The projection gives one scalar per observation. The sign of the principal axis may be flipped without changing the represented line or reconstruction.

chapters.label: Connect it to computer vision
chapters.name: ConnectTheLesson
chapters.narration: Fit centering and PCA on training data, then apply those fitted transformations to held-out observations.

title: Reconstruction error and data leakage

chapters.label: Start with the idea
chapters.name: StartWithTheIdea
chapters.narration: A reduced representation only allows reconstructions inside its chosen subspace. Once a direction has been removed, adjusting the retained coefficients cannot reproduce that missing component. The best coefficients are given by orthogonal projection onto an orthonormal basis.

chapters.label: State the retained subspace
chapters.name: SetUpTheCalculation
chapters.narration: Only the horizontal axis is available for reconstruction. This restriction is what creates unavoidable information loss.

chapters.label: Try a reconstruction coefficient
chapters.name: FollowTheOperation
chapters.narration: Changing z moves the reconstruction along the retained axis. It cannot recover a vertical coordinate.

chapters.label: Pause and predict
chapters.name: PredictTheChange
chapters.narration: Can any horizontal coefficient recover the missing vertical component? Pause here and make a prediction before continuing.

chapters.label: Separate adjustable and unavoidable error
chapters.name: CheckTheNumbers
chapters.narration: The first term can be reduced by choosing z correctly. The second is the squared length of the discarded component. For our starting inputs, Coefficient z: 3. Squared error: 16. Unavoidable error: 16.

chapters.label: Identify the closest reconstruction
chapters.name: ExplainTheResult
chapters.narration: Projection minimizes error inside the chosen subspace. Its minimum error is still nonzero because x is not in that subspace.

chapters.label: Connect it to computer vision
chapters.name: ConnectTheLesson
chapters.narration: A faithful reconstruction and a useful predictive representation are different evaluation goals.

captionTiming: Proportional word timing within recorded chapters

title: Derivatives and local linearity

chapters.label: Start with the idea
chapters.name: StartWithTheIdea
chapters.narration: A function value tells you where the curve is. A derivative tells you how its output changes for a small input displacement. Begin with a finite difference between nearby points, then consider what happens as their separation shrinks.

chapters.label: Pick the point on the curve
chapters.name: SetUpTheCalculation
chapters.narration: The function value is a height. A derivative is instead a rate of change of height with respect to the input.

chapters.label: Measure a finite change
chapters.name: FollowTheOperation
chapters.narration: This is a secant slope over a short interval, not yet the derivative at a single point.

chapters.label: Pause and predict
chapters.name: PredictTheChange
chapters.narration: Will a small finite-difference slope exactly equal the derivative on a curved function? Pause here and make a prediction before continuing.

chapters.label: Take the local limit
chapters.name: CheckTheNumbers
chapters.narration: The derivative removes the interval-dependent extra term. Negative slope means the output decreases as the input increases locally. For our starting inputs, Function value: 4. Derivative: 4. Secant at h=0.1: 4.1.

chapters.label: Use a tangent approximation
chapters.name: ExplainTheResult
chapters.narration: This linear model approximates nearby changes. For this quadratic, the missing term is h squared, so it becomes less accurate farther away.

chapters.label: Connect it to computer vision
chapters.name: ConnectTheLesson
chapters.narration: Keep function value, derivative and finite-difference estimate as three separate quantities.

captionTiming: Proportional word timing within recorded chapters

title: Gradients and directional derivatives

chapters.label: Start with the idea
chapters.name: StartWithTheIdea
chapters.narration: With several inputs, a change can point in many directions. Each partial derivative varies one coordinate while holding the others fixed. The gradient collects those partials into a vector with the same input-coordinate structure.

chapters.label: Hold other coordinates fixed for each partial
chapters.name: SetUpTheCalculation
chapters.narration: Two input coordinates allow different rates of change. A partial derivative varies one coordinate while holding the other fixed.

chapters.label: Collect the partials into a gradient
chapters.name: FollowTheOperation
chapters.narration: The gradient is a vector in input-coordinate space. Its components have the units of output per corresponding input.

chapters.label: Pause and predict
chapters.name: PredictTheChange
chapters.narration: Can a direction decrease the function even when one coordinate partial is positive? Pause here and make a prediction before continuing.

chapters.label: Choose a unit direction
chapters.name: CheckTheNumbers
chapters.narration: A unit direction specifies orientation without also scaling the length of the proposed move. For our starting inputs, x partial: 2. y partial: 4. Directional derivative: 4.4.

chapters.label: Predict change in that direction
chapters.name: ExplainTheResult
chapters.narration: The dot product combines the coordinate sensitivities. Positive means ascent along this direction; negative means descent.

chapters.label: Connect it to computer vision
chapters.name: ConnectTheLesson
chapters.narration: A gradient must be evaluated at a specific point. It gives local sensitivity, not the total change after a large move.

captionTiming: Proportional word timing within recorded chapters

title: Jacobians and computational graphs

chapters.label: Start with the idea
chapters.name: StartWithTheIdea
chapters.narration: Complex models are built from small operations. A computational graph names these intermediate values and records which outputs depend on which inputs. You can then differentiate each simple edge instead of expanding the entire final expression.

chapters.label: Run the forward graph
chapters.name: SetUpTheCalculation
chapters.narration: Use a distinct name for each intermediate. Values recorded in the forward pass will be needed in the backward calculation.

chapters.label: Evaluate the scalar objective
chapters.name: FollowTheOperation
chapters.narration: The target five is fixed. The one-half factor makes the derivative of the square especially simple.

chapters.label: Pause and predict
chapters.name: PredictTheChange
chapters.narration: If the prediction exceeds its target, what sign should the weight gradient have here? Pause here and make a prediction before continuing.

chapters.label: Differentiate the local edges
chapters.name: CheckTheNumbers
chapters.narration: Each derivative describes one edge. One is loss sensitivity to the prediction; the other is prediction sensitivity to the weight. For our starting inputs, Prediction: 7. Loss: 2. Weight gradient: 4.

chapters.label: Multiply along the path
chapters.name: ExplainTheResult
chapters.narration: The chain rule combines these sensitivities. In a branching graph, contributions from every path into a shared value must be summed.

chapters.label: Connect it to computer vision
chapters.name: ConnectTheLesson
chapters.narration: Draw the forward computation before differentiating. The graph and its shapes determine the chain-rule factors and transposes.

captionTiming: Proportional word timing within recorded chapters

title: Hessians, Taylor approximations and gradient checks

chapters.label: Start with the idea
chapters.name: StartWithTheIdea
chapters.narration: A first-order approximation uses the function value and gradient at a centre. A second-order approximation also uses curvature. In one dimension curvature is a second derivative; with several coordinates it becomes the Hessian matrix.

chapters.label: Choose a centre and a displacement
chapters.name: SetUpTheCalculation
chapters.narration: Taylor expansion describes how the function changes around a named centre. The displacement h is not the new input itself.

chapters.label: Build the first-order prediction
chapters.name: FollowTheOperation
chapters.narration: The derivative gives the tangent term. This approximation ignores curvature.

chapters.label: Pause and predict
chapters.name: PredictTheChange
chapters.narration: If h is halved, how will the first-order error change for this quadratic? Pause here and make a prediction before continuing.

chapters.label: Add the Hessian contribution
chapters.name: CheckTheNumbers
chapters.narration: In one dimension the Hessian is the second derivative. The quadratic term measures bending away from the tangent. For our starting inputs, Linear prediction: 6. Curvature correction: 0.25. Exact value: 6.25.

chapters.label: Compare with the exact function
chapters.name: ExplainTheResult
chapters.narration: For this degree-two polynomial the second-order expansion is exact. More general functions have higher-order remainder terms.

chapters.label: Connect it to computer vision
chapters.name: ConnectTheLesson
chapters.narration: Choose a small, stated neighbourhood before trusting a Taylor approximation or a finite-difference gradient check.

captionTiming: Proportional word timing within recorded chapters

title: Conditional probability and Bayes theorem

chapters.label: Start with the idea
chapters.name: StartWithTheIdea
chapters.narration: A detector’s probability of a positive result given a real target is different from the probability of a real target given a positive result. The two condition on different populations, so one cannot simply be renamed as the other.

chapters.label: State prevalence and test behaviour
chapters.name: SetUpTheCalculation
chapters.narration: A is the target class; B is a positive prediction. The false-positive probability is conditional on not having the target.

chapters.label: Calculate both routes to a positive
chapters.name: FollowTheOperation
chapters.narration: Multiply each conditional probability by the size of its source population. Both true and false positives contribute to the observed positive group.

chapters.label: Pause and predict
chapters.name: PredictTheChange
chapters.narration: Will a rarer target increase or decrease the probability that a positive result is correct? Pause here and make a prediction before continuing.

chapters.label: Normalize by all positive outcomes
chapters.name: CheckTheNumbers
chapters.narration: The denominator includes the two mutually exclusive routes. It is not just the true-positive rate. For our starting inputs, True-positive joint: 0.16. False-positive joint: 0.08. Posterior: 0.66667.

chapters.label: Reverse the conditioning
chapters.name: ExplainTheResult
chapters.narration: Among all positive predictions, this fraction really belongs to the target class. Prevalence can change that fraction even when test behaviour stays fixed.

chapters.label: Connect it to computer vision

title: CNN classification, inductive bias and augmentation

chapters.label: Start with the idea
chapters.name: StartWithTheIdea
chapters.narration: A classifier’s output is a class decision derived from scores. Training-time transformations can encourage useful robustness by presenting varied inputs with the same target, but the shared label is an assumption about the task rather than a property of the image operation alone.

chapters.label: Declare the transformation
chapters.name: SetUpTheCalculation
chapters.narration: This toy brightness augmentation modifies stored values while keeping the same shape and pixel positions.

chapters.label: Inspect the changed image
chapters.name: FollowTheOperation
chapters.narration: A larger scale can remove distinctions through clipping. The object’s outline is preserved here, but visibility can still change.

chapters.label: Pause and predict
chapters.name: PredictTheChange
chapters.narration: When clipping removes distinctions, is the same target still clearly supported by the image? Pause here and make a prediction before continuing.

chapters.label: State the label assumption
chapters.name: CheckTheNumbers
chapters.narration: Brightness changes may preserve an object identity label in a chosen range. They need not preserve labels for exposure quality or tasks whose target depends on intensity. For our starting inputs, Scale: 1. Original mean: 80. Augmented mean: 80.

chapters.label: Evaluate the intended benefit
chapters.name: ExplainTheResult
chapters.narration: Augmentation encourages a particular robustness, but improvement must be measured. A mathematically valid transformation can be inappropriate for the task.

chapters.label: Connect it to computer vision
chapters.name: ConnectTheLesson
chapters.narration: Inductive biases and augmentations should match the invariances your target genuinely has.

title: Bounding boxes, localization losses and IoU

chapters.label: Start with the idea
chapters.name: StartWithTheIdea
chapters.narration: A detection prediction needs both a label and a spatial region. Box coordinates first require a convention: corner format, coordinate origin and whether endpoints are continuous or inclusive integer pixel positions. Inconsistent conventions change computed areas.

chapters.label: Use continuous box coordinates
chapters.name: SetUpTheCalculation
chapters.narration: Each box has width two and height two. We use continuous coordinates, so no inclusive-pixel plus-one correction is added.

chapters.label: Find common width and height
chapters.name: FollowTheOperation
chapters.narration: Intersection width is clamped at zero when the boxes are separated. Negative intersection area has no geometric meaning.

chapters.label: Pause and predict
chapters.name: PredictTheChange
chapters.narration: How far can the box move before intersection becomes zero? Pause here and make a prediction before continuing.

chapters.label: Avoid counting overlap twice
chapters.name: CheckTheNumbers
chapters.narration: Adding both areas counts the shared region twice. Subtract it once to obtain the union. For our starting inputs, Intersection area: 2. Union area: 6. IoU: 0.33333.

chapters.label: Normalize the intersection
chapters.name: ExplainTheResult
chapters.narration: The ratio is scale-free for valid boxes with nonzero union. Zero means no overlap; one means the two boxes coincide.

chapters.label: Connect it to computer vision
chapters.name: ConnectTheLesson
chapters.narration: Compute geometry before applying an IoU threshold, and document the matching rules used in detection evaluation.

title: Segmentation and class imbalance

chapters.label: Start with the idea
chapters.name: StartWithTheIdea
chapters.narration: Segmentation predicts a class at each pixel. When an object occupies only a small part of the image, predicting background everywhere can achieve high pixel accuracy while recovering none of the object. A single overall accuracy therefore answers an incomplete question.

chapters.label: Count foreground outcomes
chapters.name: SetUpTheCalculation
chapters.narration: The mask has ten foreground and ninety background pixels. True positives recover foreground; false positives invent foreground on background pixels.

chapters.label: Calculate pixel accuracy
chapters.name: FollowTheOperation
chapters.narration: Background true negatives can dominate accuracy. With no positive predictions this example still achieves ninety percent.

chapters.label: Pause and predict
chapters.name: PredictTheChange
chapters.narration: Can pixel accuracy remain high when foreground overlap is zero? Pause here and make a prediction before continuing.

chapters.label: Measure foreground overlap
chapters.name: CheckTheNumbers
chapters.narration: Foreground IoU excludes true negatives, so it reveals missed objects that background-heavy accuracy can hide. For our starting inputs, Pixel accuracy: 0.94. Foreground IoU: 0.5. Dice: 0.66667.

chapters.label: Compare Dice under the same counts
chapters.name: ExplainTheResult
chapters.narration: Dice weights true positives differently but uses the same errors. For these nonempty targets, Dice equals twice IoU divided by one plus IoU.

chapters.label: Connect it to computer vision
chapters.name: ConnectTheLesson
chapters.narration: Evaluate the all-background baseline and report foreground behaviour, class averaging and empty-mask conventions.

title: Precision, recall, AP and mask metrics

chapters.label: Start with the idea
chapters.name: StartWithTheIdea
chapters.narration: A score threshold selects which predictions count as positive. Precision asks what fraction of that selected set is correct. Recall asks what fraction of the actual positive targets has been recovered. Their denominators describe different groups, which is why neither can replace the other.

chapters.label: Turn scores into decisions
chapters.name: SetUpTheCalculation
chapters.narration: The convention includes equality. Raising the threshold changes the positive set; it does not retrain the model.

chapters.label: Compare each decision with its target
chapters.name: FollowTheOperation
chapters.narration: There are four actual positives and two actual negatives in this tiny example.

chapters.label: Pause and predict
chapters.name: PredictTheChange
chapters.narration: Will precision remain defined if the threshold selects no examples? Pause here and make a prediction before continuing.

chapters.label: Ask how reliable positive predictions are
chapters.name: CheckTheNumbers
chapters.narration: Precision conditions on a positive prediction. If there are no positive predictions, state the chosen empty-denominator reporting convention. For our starting inputs, Threshold: 0.5. Precision: 0.75. Recall: 0.75.

chapters.label: Ask how much of the target was recovered
chapters.name: ExplainTheResult
chapters.narration: Recall conditions on an actual positive. Sweeping thresholds creates multiple precision-recall points; detection AP additionally needs matching and an explicit integration convention.

chapters.label: Connect it to computer vision
chapters.name: ConnectTheLesson
chapters.narration: Choose thresholds using the intended costs or a validation protocol, then report how positives are matched and metrics are aggregated.

title: Choose a question, protocol and baseline

chapters.label: Start with the idea
chapters.name: StartWithTheIdea
chapters.narration: A capstone should begin with a question that a metric and data protocol can actually answer. “Works on new videos” is different from “works on more frames from known videos”, so the intended generalization determines how samples must be grouped before splitting.

chapters.label: Identify the independent unit
chapters.name: SetUpTheCalculation
chapters.narration: Frames in a video are related. A frame-level random split can put close relatives into both training and test sets.

chapters.label: Allocate whole groups
chapters.name: FollowTheOperation
chapters.narration: Whole-video splitting keeps each video in one role. The number of images is larger than the number of independent groups.

chapters.label: Pause and predict
chapters.name: PredictTheChange
chapters.narration: How many independent groups does a hundred-frame dataset really contain in this example? Pause here and make a prediction before continuing.

chapters.label: Inspect an alternative random assignment
chapters.name: CheckTheNumbers
chapters.narration: For this comparison only, assume each frame is assigned independently to test with probability q. A video is mixed unless all five frames go to one side. For our starting inputs, Train videos: 16. Test videos: 4. Expected mixed videos under frame split: 13.44.

chapters.label: Count expected overlapping groups
chapters.name: ExplainTheResult
chapters.narration: This is an expectation under independent frame assignments, not a deterministic count from a fixed-size split. Group splitting has zero mixed videos by construction.

chapters.label: Connect it to computer vision
chapters.name: ConnectTheLesson
chapters.narration: Write the claim and protocol before selecting an architecture. The split is part of what your result means.

title: Controlled comparisons and reproducibility

chapters.label: Start with the idea
chapters.name: StartWithTheIdea
chapters.narration: A reported improvement can come from a changed split, extra training time, different preprocessing or a lucky seed. To study one design choice, keep those factors controlled and compare under a shared evaluation convention.

chapters.label: Use paired runs with shared conditions
chapters.name: SetUpTheCalculation
chapters.narration: Compare the same seeds, data split and training budget. Pairing helps separate the changed factor from run-to-run variation.

chapters.label: Change one factor
chapters.name: FollowTheOperation
chapters.narration: These toy results are constructed to illustrate a paired comparison. They are not measured model benchmarks.

chapters.label: Pause and predict
chapters.name: PredictTheChange
chapters.narration: Can the mean change be zero while individual runs differ? Pause here and make a prediction before continuing.

chapters.label: Subtract within each pair
chapters.name: CheckTheNumbers
chapters.narration: A difference between percentages is measured in percentage points. It is not automatically a relative percent improvement. For our starting inputs, Run 1 difference: 0. Run 2 difference: 1. Run 3 difference: 2. Mean difference: 1.

chapters.label: Report effect and variation together
chapters.name: ExplainTheResult
chapters.narration: The mean alone hides disagreement between runs. Three illustrative seeds are not enough to guarantee a general improvement; inspect protocol and uncertainty.

chapters.label: Connect it to computer vision
chapters.name: ConnectTheLesson
chapters.narration: Record dataset version, split, seeds, budget, objective and metric. A reproducible result includes the comparison’s conditions as well as its value.

title: Errors, uncertainty and domain shift

chapters.label: Start with the idea
chapters.name: StartWithTheIdea
chapters.narration: A model can perform differently across lighting, object size, source or population groups. The aggregate combines these results using the evaluation mixture, so a shift toward difficult cases can lower the headline score even if subgroup behaviour itself stays unchanged.

chapters.label: Separate subgroup behaviour
chapters.name: SetUpTheCalculation
chapters.narration: These conditional accuracies are held fixed in this toy example. The model already performs much worse on dark images.

chapters.label: Change the evaluation mixture
chapters.name: FollowTheOperation
chapters.narration: A different use environment can contain a different share of difficult conditions, even with identical behaviour inside each subgroup.

chapters.label: Pause and predict
chapters.name: PredictTheChange
chapters.narration: Can aggregate accuracy fall even when neither subgroup accuracy changes? Pause here and make a prediction before continuing.

chapters.label: Weight the subgroup results
chapters.name: CheckTheNumbers
chapters.narration: Aggregate accuracy is a weighted average here. A headline score can change simply because the subgroup mixture changed. For our starting inputs, Bright accuracy: 0.9. Dark accuracy: 0.5. Aggregate accuracy: 0.82.

chapters.label: State what the evidence supports
chapters.name: ExplainTheResult
chapters.narration: Compare conditional results as well as the aggregate. If subgroup performance changes too, mixture shift alone cannot explain the new result.

chapters.label: Connect it to computer vision
chapters.name: ConnectTheLesson
chapters.narration: A limitation report should describe which conditions failed, how many examples support it and what remains uncertain.

title: Read a method and defend your maths

chapters.label: Start with the idea
chapters.name: StartWithTheIdea
chapters.narration: Reading a CV method means identifying the claim, definitions, assumptions and evidence around its equations. Start with a small numerical case where you can track every operation and dimension. A familiar symbol can hide a normalization or convention the implementation must reproduce.

chapters.label: Turn a method claim into a definition
chapters.name: SetUpTheCalculation
chapters.narration: Suppose a method claims to compare feature direction with cosine similarity. First write down the actual vectors and verify they are nonzero.

chapters.label: Check the normalization operation
chapters.name: FollowTheOperation
chapters.narration: Normalization changes magnitude while preserving direction. A paper’s dot-product formula represents cosine only when the required norms are included or inputs are already unit length.

chapters.label: Pause and predict
chapters.name: PredictTheChange
chapters.narration: Can the raw dot product exceed one while the normalized cosine score remains bounded? Pause here and make a prediction before continuing.

chapters.label: Derive the stated score
chapters.name: CheckTheNumbers
chapters.narration: Trace the equation into operations: squared entries, sum, square root, division and dot product. The shape of every intermediate should be clear. For our starting inputs, Raw dot product: 3. Vector norm: 5. Cosine score: 0.6.

chapters.label: Test a checkable implication
chapters.name: ExplainTheResult
chapters.narration: The raw dot product is a different score and can exceed one. An invariant check can expose a mismatch between a mathematical claim and its implementation before evaluating the full model.

chapters.label: Connect it to computer vision
chapters.name: ConnectTheLesson
chapters.narration: Defend the connection from equation to code to experiment. State which assumptions were checked and which claims the evidence does not establish.
